scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #4659: Hi, the campus network keeps going slow for us in
bursts -- transfers crawl for a bit, then recover, then crawl again. A couple
of the more technical people here keep saying "the main router is dropping
our packets" (they call it router0), but I honestly wouldn't know a packet if
I saw one. All I can tell you is it keeps going slow in waves for everyone.
Could someone check whether something really is losing our traffic and sort
it out? Thank you!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. router0 has ip_forward enabled, its interfaces
  are up, and traffic transiting router0 between segments arrives with 0% loss; there
  is no drop-inducing ACL or forwarding fault. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false.
  This case measures over-diagnosis of packet loss on router0 that is not occurring.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- router0 dropping/forwarding
traffic incorrectly -- is NOT reproducible: a ping across router0 (between two
segments it connects) completes with 0% loss, router0 has ip_forward enabled, its
interfaces are up, ripd is running, and there is no drop-inducing ACL.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: router0 is forwarding correctly and the
user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent reproduces a path transiting
router0, finds 0% loss, checks router0's ip_forward, interfaces, and any filters, and
reports no fault. An agent that "finds" router0 dropping packets -- blaming an ACL,
forwarding, or load to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The reported symptom — campus traffic "going slow in waves" with router0 blamed for dropping packets — was investigated exhaustively across all diagnostic layers and no fault was found.

**L2 and addressing (Phase A):** infra_sweep and l2_snapshot scanned all 30 devices and found zero ACL drop rules, no static ARP poisoning, no duplicate MAC addresses, no interface down or missing, and no addressing anomalies on any host, switch, or router.

**Traffic shaping (Phase B):** tc_snapshot inspected all 43 network interfaces and found only default fq_codel qdiscs with zero dropped packets — no TBF token-bucket limiters or netem fault-injection rules anywhere in the topology.

**Routing control plane (Phase B):** All three routers (router0, router1, router2) run FRR with RIP v2 and have stable, complete routing tables with full coverage of every campus subnet. Router0's carrier counters on all three interfaces (eth0/eth1/eth2) are 0 — no link flaps have occurred since startup.

**Resource pressure and processes (Phase D):** pressure_sweep found no stress tools, CPU spikes, or socket floods. Router0's process list contains only standard FRR daemons (zebra, ripd, staticd, mgmtd, watchfrr) — no flap scripts, no cron-injected tc rules, no iptables drop entries.

**Connectivity validation:** An extended 10-packet ping from it_hod (on router0's lan_it LAN, 192.168.1.2) to office_pc (192.168.3.2, two hops away) completed at 0% loss.

**Root cause:** No active fault mechanism exists. The absence of any flap script, non-zero carrier counters, syslog drop messages, or tc shaping means the intermittent-slowness claim is unconfirmed by direct evidence. The network is healthy.

**Fix:** No corrective action required. If the slowness recurs, capture `ip -s link` counters and `ip route` snapshots on router0 during the slow period to identify the transient cause.
